Flexible, but Not Free

The hidden cost of gig work for Toronto polytechnic students

Written in Toronto
Toronto, Student Life, Systems Thinking, Economics

Every gig platform promises the same bargain: work whenever you want, earn on your own schedule, keep complete freedom over your week. When you're studying full-time in a city as expensive as Toronto, that pitch sounds like the perfect arrangement.

If you have a networking lab at George Brown on Monday morning, a routing assignment due Tuesday night and an exam on Friday, traditional shift work is hard to fit around classes. App-based work seems to solve that by letting you log on whenever there's a gap.

Over time, though, you notice the flexibility isn't actually free. The cost just shows up somewhere else — in fragmented attention, physical wear, and the slow erosion of deep study time.

Three hours aren't three hours

On paper, three separate one-hour gaps look the same as one three-hour block. In practice they aren't close. Studying subnetting, fixing a broken Linux DHCP config or building a multi-VM Active Directory lab needs uninterrupted focus just to load the problem into your head.

When the day is split between traffic, notifications and short shifts, you never really get there. Even after you sit back down, it takes a while before you're thinking clearly again.

The costs you don't see on payday

The money can be just as misleading if you only look at gross payouts. Fuel, maintenance, tires, insurance and depreciation happen in the background, so you rarely feel them on the day you get paid.

The bigger cost is opportunity: every tired evening spent recovering from scattered shifts is an evening not spent on lab work, on finishing Network+, or on projects that move a career forward for good.

Protecting the work that compounds

Living and studying here means being practical — bills have to be paid. What changed things for me was treating study blocks and lab time with the same seriousness as a scheduled job.

Batching work into predictable days instead of letting it leak into every free hour makes the difference. Real flexibility doesn't come from an app letting you pick when to go online. It comes from building skills solid enough to give you real options later.
